extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and tertiary mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating students' comprehension of mathematical proofs (especially comparisons between linear and Leron-style structured proofs) using multi-dimensional assessment items and experimental measures. Includes guidance for producing structured proofs (levels, elevator) and noted pitfalls for reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of this type assess whether students can justify how a new statement in a proof follows from previous assertions as well as how a particular statement is used to justify subsequent statements within the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one of the proof-comprehension dimensions in Mejia-Ramos et al.'s assessment model. In the study, structured-proof readers performed slightly (but not statistically reliably) worse on questions concerning justifications. Items should probe both backward (why does this follow?) and forward (how is this used later?) justificatory relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of this type assess whether students can recognize the overarching ideas used in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 1 of a structured proof is essentially a summary and is theoretically designed to aid this competency. The study found that participants reading structured proofs were better at identifying a good summary (eg. Only Zero proof: 76% structured vs. 63% linear, statistically reliable). However, many students failed to understand Level 1 when it was unclear, so summaries must be clear and accessible to confer benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of this type assess whether students can apply the ideas used in the proof in a new setting to prove a new theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured proofs (via Level 1 and the between-levels 'elevator') are theoretically intended to support transfer by revealing the method. In the quantitative study, structured-proof readers performed slightly (but not statistically reliably) worse on transfer items for some proofs; transfer should be measured by tasks requiring applying the method to novel but related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration with examples / Diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of this type assess whether students can relate the chain of argumentation in a proof to a particular example (i.e., transform the formal proof into a generic proof) or a relevant diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses ability to instantiate abstract reasoning in concrete examples or visuals. The study reports structured-proof readers performed slightly worse (not statistically reliably) on items concerning illustration with examples. Items can ask for a specific example, a constructed counterexample, or a diagram that captures the proof's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven-dimension proof-comprehension model (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assessment model for proof comprehension developed by Mejia-Ramos et al. (2010) that identifies seven different ways to assess students' understanding of a proof; four of these were used in the quantitative study (Justification, Summary, Transfer, Illustration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model is explicitly non-hierarchical: separate dimensions should be measured independently because a presentation style might help some dimensions while hindering others. The paper describes rationale and schemes for generating questions of each type (see Mejia-Ramos et al. for full list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reported understanding (Likert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were asked 'How well do you feel you understand this proof?' recorded on a five-point Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used alongside objective comprehension items to capture perceived understanding. Can reveal differences between subjective impressions and objective performance; useful as an auxiliary metric when interpreting effects of presentation format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference / liking of format (Likert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants in a structured condition were asked to report the extent to which they liked the format in which the proof had been presented using a three-point Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides attitudinal data about format acceptability; note that dislike (e.g., due to 'jumping around') does not necessarily correlate with objective comprehension gains. Use to interpret implementation feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured proof format: Levels and 'elevator' (production guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leron's structured proofs present proofs in levels: Level 1 provides a summary of the main ideas; Level 2 summarizes how each main idea will be implemented; successively lower levels fill in details. Some structured proofs include an 'elevator' between levels providing rationale for choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The format is intended to give readers a high-level schema without losing access to full logical detail; Level 1 aids summary and method-recognition, and the elevator clarifies motivations (example: Triadic Primes proof). When producing structured proofs: explicitly state Level 1 aims, provide clear between-level rationales, and ensure lower-level details are accessible for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity/Accessibility of Level 1 (production & evaluative note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level 1 must be comprehensible as a high-level summary; if students fail to understand Level 1 they may integrate details into an inappropriate framework or experience cognitive overload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: many participants could not understand Level 1 and thus failed to benefit from it. To mitigate, make Level 1 explicit and unambiguous, define key terms right before the theorem (e.g., 'triadic prime'), and consider instructional scaffolding or prior exposure to the structured format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'jumping around' cognitive load (anti-pattern / evaluative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured proofs inherently require readers to move between levels and sections, which can force readers to keep multiple ideas in working memory and 'jump around' the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'jumping' was frequently reported as decreasing comprehension and increasing reading time. Mitigations include: keeping related information nearer to one another, clarifying cross-references, using arrows/visual cues, providing instructions about how to read structured proofs, and giving students practice with the format. Note that 'jumping' may sometimes aid making connections, so evaluate tradeoffs per target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with argument form / domain knowledge (evaluative moderator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' prior familiarity with the type of argumentation or domain affects their ability to use a structured proof's high-level skeleton to understand details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation: participants familiar with the argument type (e.g., calculus/Rolle's theorem) could absorb a structured proof despite format novelty; those unfamiliar (e.g., number theory skeleton) struggled. When assessing or deploying structured proofs, consider participants' background and provide additional scaffolding where domain familiarity is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation instructions / preparatory scaffolding (intervention guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing explicit instructions about the nature and purposes of structured proofs before reading can affect comprehension and attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, one group received instructions describing structured proofs; some evidence suggested instruction did not always improve objective performance (Structured-No Directions outperformed Structured-With Directions on most items), but instructions may reduce misconceptions about the format. Use clear preparatory guidance and test whether it aids your population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place less-significant lemmas lower in the structure (production convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convention of structured proofs is placing proofs of lemmas or less-significant details near the end (lower levels) to reflect their relative lack of importance to the main line of argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should be aware readers may expect the final line to state the theorem; explicitly indicate how the structure maps to the logical conclusion to avoid confusion that 'nothing was proved'. Consider labeling concluding lines and linking them to Level 1 claims to reduce misinterpretation.
